# Evaluating AI-for-Architecture Claims: A Guide for Reviewers and Researchers {#sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist}

When evaluating research publications, benchmark proposals, or engineering design reports in AI-assisted and AI-native computer architecture, the central challenge is separating genuine microarchitectural innovation from tool gaming, uncalibrated proxies, and mismatched tuning budgets. Rather than imposing a mechanical compliance checklist or rigid scoring rubric, this guide synthesizes the principles established throughout this monograph into actionable evaluation criteria. It is organized directly around the three primary AI method families introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization (generative synthesis, predictive surrogates, and closed-loop optimization) and their vertical orchestration within real design workflows (@sec-running-the-loop; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).

Reviewers, researchers, and students can use these criteria to probe the methodological rigor, physical grounding, and reproducibility of architectural claims.

## 1. Evaluating Generative Methods: Code, HDL, and Circuit Synthesis

Generative techniques use foundation models, transformer code generators, or template-based prompting to generate hardware description language (HDL) modules, SystemVerilog assertions, testbenches, or microarchitectural glue logic.

### Physical Signoff versus Syntactic Validity
- **The Pitfall:** Papers frequently claim high success rates (such as "95% Pass@1") based solely on whether generated register-transfer level (RTL) code compiles or passes a superficial unit-level testbench simulation. Such metrics overlook critical downstream physical signoff failures.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Does the generated code pass strict linting, clock-domain crossing (CDC) verification, and formal equivalence checking against reference specifications?
  - Does the synthesized netlist achieve timing closure without introducing unconstrained latches, combinational feedback loops, or illegal asynchronous reset structures?
  - When pushed through place-and-route in a modern process node (such as OpenROAD or commercial electronic design automation (EDA) toolchains), does the layout satisfy design rule check (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) requirements?
- **Sound Evidence:** Reporting complete EDA signoff metrics (setup/hold slack, total negative slack, cell area, dynamic power, and DRC violation counts) using standard cell libraries under declared process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, rather than simulation-only testbench passes.

### Benchmark Contamination and Memorization
- **The Pitfall:** Autoregressive models trained on public code repositories routinely memorize public hardware benchmarks (such as VerilogEval, RTLLM, or basic arithmetic blocks), producing inflated scores that fail to transfer to novel design problems.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Did the authors evaluate contamination against their pretraining and fine-tuning corpora, identifying exact and near-duplicate overlaps with test prompts [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated]?
  - Is the evaluation conducted on held-out, parameterized, or proprietary tasks that were strictly created after the model's training data cutoff?
  - Does the method generalize to unseen domain-specific instruction set architecture (ISA) extensions, non-standard bus protocols, or custom packaging constraints?
- **Sound Evidence:** Conducting explicit data decontamination audits, reporting performance on novel industrial-grade modules with withheld interface definitions, and evaluating zero-shot generalization across structurally distinct microarchitectures.

### Human Steering and the True Cost of Repair
- **The Pitfall:** Papers often celebrate automated drafting speedups (such as generating an accelerator block in seconds) while omitting the extensive human engineering hours required to craft multi-turn prompt templates, diagnose syntax errors, and manually patch subtle timing glitches.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - What human engineering effort was invested in prompt engineering, prompt refinement, error triage, and manual post-generation code editing?
  - When accounting for human verification and manual qualification time, does the workflow achieve a net project-level speedup under Amdahl's Law of design pipelines (@sec-data-scarcity-verification-load)?
- **Sound Evidence:** Transparently logging human interaction time, prompt iteration counts, and manual repair interventions, comparing total engineering hours against an unassisted senior design team.

## 2. Evaluating Predictive and Surrogate Models: Timing, Power, and Latent Spaces

Predictive methods use learned models (such as graph neural networks (GNNs), gradient-boosted trees, or neural surrogate regressors) to approximate expensive physical simulations, predicting wire delays, power dissipation, routing congestion, or cache miss rates.

### Local Ranking Fidelity versus Global Aggregate Error
- **The Pitfall:** A surrogate model may achieve high aggregate $R^2$ or low root-mean-square error (RMSE) across a broad, randomly sampled architectural space, yet exhibit zero or negative rank correlation in the top 1% candidate region where optimization algorithms actually concentrate (the Optimizer's Curse, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Does the paper report ranking fidelity metrics (such as Kendall's $\tau$ or Spearman's $\rho$) specifically within the high-performing candidate subset, or only averaged across the entire training distribution?
  - When the surrogate identifies the "top 10" candidate architectures, do those specific designs remain Pareto-optimal when verified with high-fidelity signoff tools?
- **Sound Evidence:** Reporting top-$k$ recall curves and rank correlation coefficients restricted to the active search boundary, demonstrating that the surrogate correctly orders high-performing candidates rather than merely separating good designs from broken ones.

### Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Physical Drift
- **The Pitfall:** Surrogates trained on a specific process technology (such as 28\ nm planar CMOS), fixed aspect ratio, or specific floorplan density fail silently when extrapolated to advanced FinFET/GAAFET nodes, novel 2.5D/3D chiplet interconnects, or higher clock frequencies.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - What are the explicit physical boundaries of the surrogate's validity region, and does the paper test architectures outside that training envelope?
  - Does the model incorporate physics-informed constraints (such as RC wire delay scaling, power-grid IR-drop limits, or thermal dissipation equations) to bound out-of-distribution predictions?
- **Sound Evidence:** Measuring prediction accuracy across technology node transfers, unseen floorplan aspect ratios, and varying operating voltages, accompanied by automated uncertainty quantification that flags when candidate evaluations leave the training manifold.

### Latent Space Grounding and Decodability
- **The Pitfall:** Performing optimization in continuous learned latent representations (such as graph embeddings or autoencoder manifolds) often generates latent points that decode to unroutable geometries, disconnected clock nets, or physically impossible microarchitectural topologies.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Does every valid point in the latent space decode deterministically to a physically legal, synthesizable hardware representation (@tbl-latent-space-map)?
  - How does the decoding pipeline handle constraint violations and geometric overlaps during physical reconstruction?
- **Sound Evidence:** Demonstrating 100% legal reconstruction rates across the evaluated latent space, verifying that decoded candidates pass DRC/LVS physical signoff without manual repair.

## 3. Evaluating Optimization and Search Loops: Reinforcement Learning, Bayesian Methods, and Design-Space Exploration

Optimization methods employ reinforcement learning (RL), Bayesian optimization (BO), evolutionary algorithms, or Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) to explore large microarchitectural parameter spaces, autotuning floorplans, cache hierarchies, or compiler schedules in design-space exploration (DSE).

### Baseline Parity and the Strawman Trap
- **The Pitfall:** Comparing an advanced AI search framework that consumed 500 GPU-hours against an untuned classical heuristic (such as default simulated annealing or unguided random search) executed for 10 minutes on a single CPU core.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Is the proposed method compared against the strongest practical conventional baseline (such as expert-tuned commercial EDA autotuners, heavily budget-matched simulated annealing, or multi-start Bayesian optimization)?
  - Were all comparison arms allocated strictly identical compute budgets, simulator execution limits, and hyperparameter tuning effort (@tbl-matched-system-comparison)?
- **Sound Evidence:** Providing budget-matched comparison curves showing quality-of-results (QoR) as a function of total wall-clock time, consumed CPU/GPU compute hours, and simulator license invocations for every evaluated algorithm.

### Proxy Exploitation and Simulator Loopholes
- **The Pitfall:** Autonomous search algorithms aggressively exploit inaccuracies, omitted corner cases, or missing physical constraints in fast simulators, discovering "super-optimal" candidates that achieve record benchmark scores by gaming the simulation harness. Common exploits include omitting DRAM refresh cycles, ignoring cache coherence traffic, or violating bus handshake wait states.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Did the winning candidate architectures undergo independent verification in a higher-fidelity execution environment (such as cycle-accurate RTL simulation in Verilator, field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation in FireSim, or post-layout gate-level timing)?
  - Did the authors implement invariant assertion checkers and anti-gaming penalties to prevent the optimizer from modifying constraint scripts, relaxing timing bounds, or bypassing memory consistency rules?
- **Sound Evidence:** Validating final optimized designs across multiple independent simulation layers, confirming that reported performance improvements persist under cycle-accurate hardware emulation and gate-level physical verification.

### Multi-Objective Trade-Offs and Constraint Integrity
- **The Pitfall:** Claiming significant speedup on a primary performance metric while silently sacrificing unrewarded physical constraints, such as exceeding thermal design power (TDP), blowing out static random-access memory (SRAM) area budgets, or inducing severe voltage droop.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Does the evaluation report the complete multi-objective Pareto vector (power, performance, area, thermal dissipation, and access latency) at identical operating points?
  - Are hard physical constraints treated as non-negotiable boundaries, with candidate designs that violate any single constraint classified as invalid?
- **Sound Evidence:** Plotting full Pareto frontiers across multiple competing objectives, explicitly displaying constraint boundary limits and proving that all advancing candidates satisfy thermal, electrical, and area signoff requirements.

## 4. Evaluating System-Level Orchestration and Tool Infrastructure

AI-native design systems combine multiple generative, predictive, and optimization tools into automated closed loops. Evaluating these end-to-end workflows requires scrutinizing reproducibility, total cost accounting, and governance.

### Lineage, State Provenance, and Deterministic Replay
- **The Pitfall:** Publishing experimental results that cannot be replayed or audited because model weights rely on floating commercial API aliases (`model-latest`), random seeds were omitted, or tool runtime container environments were undocumented.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Are all tool versions, EDA script flags, container image digests (`sha256:...`), and random seeds explicitly declared?
  - When commercial foundation models are used, did the authors record exact checkpoint dates, temperature settings, and raw prompt-response transcripts?
- **Sound Evidence:** Releasing versioned container receipts, fixed seed logs, and cryptographic execution hashes that allow independent reviewers to re-execute the entire exploration workflow from intent to signoff.

### Comprehensive Economic and License Accounting
- **The Pitfall:** Reporting only the compute required for the single winning execution run, while concealing the hundreds of crashed runs, failed synthesis attempts, discarded exploration branches, and commercial EDA license fees consumed during development.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Does the paper report the total gross cost of exploration, including failed, timed-out, and pruned candidate evaluations?
  - Does the economic model balance cheap token generation against the scarce, expensive EDA licenses required to verify those generated candidates (@sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search)?
- **Sound Evidence:** Publishing complete attempt cost records (@tbl-attempt-cost-record) detailing total token usage, cloud compute spend, EDA license-hours, and wall-clock execution elapsed time across all exploratory and confirmation phases.

### Technical Ownership and Decision Authority
- **The Pitfall:** Conflating automated candidate proposal with engineering signoff, or claiming an autonomous AI system "designed, verified, and taped out" a production processor without human architectural oversight.
- **Critical Questions:**
  - Who holds named commitment authority for advancing candidates between life-cycle stages and authorizing physical tapeout (@sec-what-architect-owns)?
  - How does the workflow present multi-candidate Pareto trade-offs and residual risks to human architects to prevent ceremonial rubber-stamping?
- **Sound Evidence:** Explicitly defining the governance structure and action rights (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights), clearly separating automated proposal generation from non-delegable human commitment authority.

## 5. Summary Evaluation Matrix

Reviewers and researchers can use the consolidated evaluation matrix (@tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix) to assess whether an architectural contribution provides defensible evidence or exhibits common red-flag failure modes across each method family.

| **Method Family** | **Primary Evaluation Target** | **Required Technical Evidence** | **Common Red Flags & Pitfalls** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Generative Synthesis** *(HDL, RTL, Assertions)* | Physical realizability and design correctness | Full EDA signoff (STA setup/hold, CDC, DRC/LVS, power) under declared PVT corners. | Compilation-only evaluation; benchmark suite contamination; unrecorded manual repair hours. |
| **Predictive Surrogates** *(Timing, Power, Latents)* | Ranking accuracy in the active search region | Top-$k$ rank correlation ($\tau$, $\rho$) on high-performing candidates; out-of-distribution transfer tests. | High global $R^2$ masking top-$k$ inversion (Optimizer's Curse); ungrounded latent spaces. |
| **Optimization Loops** *(RL, BO, DSE)* | Search efficiency and constraint integrity | Matched-budget comparisons against tuned conventional heuristics; full Pareto frontier reporting. | Mismatched compute budgets; simulator loophole exploitation; unconstrained thermal/power violations. |
| **System Orchestration** *(Multi-Tool Closed Loops)* | End-to-end reproducibility and governance | Pinned container digests; complete license/token cost accounting; human commitment boundaries. | Floating model endpoints; finalist-only cost reporting; automated systems claiming tapeout authority. |
: **The AI-for-Architecture Evaluation Matrix.** A structured guide for assessing generative, predictive, optimization, and system-level claims in computer architecture research and engineering. {#tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix tbl-colwidths="[18,26,30,26]"}
